tagline: AI, chips and the companies building the future.

articles.title: Qualcomm Falls on Revenue Miss and Weak Guidance as Arm Beats but Stays Cautious
articles.description: Qualcomm shares fell more than 6% after hours after a revenue miss and soft guidance, while Arm beat estimates with data-centre royalties doubling — but its cautious outlook also left investors wanting more.
articles.sources: SiliconANGLE, Loomi.Ai, TipRanks, November 4-5, 2026
articles.body:
Chipmakers Qualcomm and Arm Holdings reported results after the market closed on Wednesday, November 4, and both left investors wanting more — a day after Advanced Micro Devices delivered an impressive earnings beat that had raised expectations for the whole sector, SiliconANGLE reported.

Qualcomm: a miss on revenue, a soft guide

Qualcomm reported fiscal fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of $2.17 per share on revenue of $10.44 billion, up just 8 percent from a year earlier. Wall Street had expected earnings of $2.16 per share on sales of $10.48 billion, so the result was mixed — but the stock fell more than 6 percent in after-hours trading on the revenue miss and weak guidance. For the current quarter, Qualcomm guided to earnings of around $2.25 per share at the midpoint on sales of $10.48 billion, short of the Street’s target of $2.27 per share. Smartphone chip sales fell 26 percent in the quarter to $5.14 billion, behind the $5.21 billion analysts expected, despite the company raising prices on its own chips recently.

The bright spots: cars and the Internet of Things

Qualcomm’s automotive business was the standout, with sales rising 89 percent to $1.99 billion, well above the $1.66 billion consensus estimate. Internet of Things revenue came to $1.88 billion, up 4 percent from a year ago and just ahead of estimates, while revenue from the company’s licensing segment rose to $650 million. The automotive strength shows Qualcomm’s diversification beyond phones is working, but cars remain dwarfed by the smartphone business, which still drives the bulk of revenue.

Arm beats — then disappoints on guidance

Arm delivered more palatable results: adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, just beating the Street’s target of 48 cents, while revenue rose 27 percent from a year earlier to $1.44 billion, ahead of the $1.38 billion analysts expected. The company said its data-centre business was the main growth driver this year, with royalties there doubling year over year. But its guidance did little to excite investors, and the stock was down about 2 percent in late trading. Arm guided to earnings of 56 cents per share, plus or minus four cents, against Wall Street’s forecast of 55 cents, and revenue of $1.54 billion, plus or minus $50 million, just ahead of the $1.52 billion Street target. GlobalFoundries did a little better than its peers, posting third-quarter adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on sales of $1.9 billion, up 12 percent, with growth driven by AI and data-centre demand. The pattern of the week is now clear: in a market repricing AI spending, even a beat is not enough unless the outlook excites — and Qualcomm’s miss shows how quickly sentiment can turn.

articles.title: Nvidia's November 17 Earnings: the $108 Billion Test That Will Set the AI Trade's Tone
articles.description: Nvidia reports third-quarter results on November 17, guided to $108 billion in revenue, with analysts expecting about $109 billion — the most important AI earnings report of the quarter after a brutal chip selloff.
articles.sources: JorgAI, Intellectia, Tickeron, November 2026
articles.body:
Nvidia reports its third quarter of fiscal 2027 on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, after the market closes, with the earnings call at 2:00 p.m. Pacific, 5:00 p.m. Eastern, according to the company’s October 28 notice. It is the most anticipated earnings report of the quarter — the last big AI print before the Federal Reserve’s December meeting, and the one investors say will decide whether the recent chip selloff is a correction or something more severe.

The bar Nvidia set for itself

The numbers to be judged against come from Nvidia’s August 26 release: second-quarter revenue was $96.2 billion, with data-centre revenue of $89.0 billion, and the company’s own third-quarter outlook reads, word for word, “Revenue is expected to be $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%. NVIDIA is not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in its outlook,” with gross margins expected at 74.0 percent, plus or minus 50 basis points. Analysts expect revenue of about $109.17 billion and earnings of $2.48 per share, compared with $1.30 per share and $57.01 billion in the prior-year period, according to reports. The stock’s first full reaction comes on Wednesday, November 18.

A $279 billion footnote

Nvidia’s most important number before the report may not be revenue at all, according to one analysis: it is $279 billion, the supply and capacity commitments disclosed in the company’s latest 10-Q, up from $119 billion one quarter earlier. The schedule shows $92 billion due in the remainder of fiscal 2027, $87 billion in fiscal 2028 and $88 billion in fiscal 2029, with only $12 billion after that — about 96 percent landing within roughly two and a half years. Chief financial officer Colette Kress said the increase was primarily related to the procurement of memory, and that margins should trough at 71 to 72 percent in the fourth quarter, partly because of memory costs, while she expects about 70 percent revenue growth in fiscal 2028. The company also disclosed guarantees capped at $105 billion supporting a 4.25-gigawatt build at SB Energy’s Ohio campus.

Why this report matters so much

Nvidia is the largest single stock in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100, so its guidance sets Wednesday’s tone for the whole market. It comes a month after TSMC’s record quarter — the foundry that makes Nvidia’s chips — so the demand side is partly known. And it arrives after a brutal stretch: Nvidia shares have fallen roughly 13.6 percent over the last 30 days, from about $233.95 to $202.06, as a broad AI-chip selloff pressured the sector, while Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan warned that capital and funding — not chip or power shortages — could become the main constraint on AI expansion. If Nvidia’s guidance disappoints or management hints at any demand softness, the stock could face significant selling pressure given its large index weighting. If the Blackwell ramp looks strong and the Vera Rubin platform is on track, it could restore confidence across the semiconductor supply chain. History suggests a big move either way: across 67 Nvidia earnings reports since 2010, the stock closed up the next session 37 times and down 30, with a median swing of 4.9 percent in either direction.

articles.title: AMD Revenue Jumps 45% to $13.38 Billion as Data Centre Sales Nearly Double
articles.description: AMD reported third-quarter revenue of $13.38 billion, up 45%, beating estimates, with data centre revenue surging 97% to $8.5 billion — and guided to about $17 billion for the holiday quarter.
articles.sources: AMD results via Sharesify, Global Insight, InvestingLive, TickerRoast, November 3-4, 2026
articles.body:
Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter 2026 results after the market closed on Tuesday, November 3, with revenue rising 45 percent year over year to $13.38 billion, above the roughly $13.09 billion analysts expected, and adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share against a $1.95 forecast, reports said.

The data centre engine

Data centre revenue surged 97 percent to about $8.5 billion, up from $4.34 billion a year earlier, and now accounts for roughly 64 percent of AMD's total revenue, driven by Instinct AI accelerators and EPYC server processors. Gaming revenue fell 40 percent year over year to $773 million, though that still beat the $655 million analysts expected. Shares rose about 6 to 7 percent in after-hours trading, recovering part of a slide that had seen the stock fall for three straight sessions on worries about AI spending.

A bold 2027 signal

For the fourth quarter, AMD forecast revenue of about $17 billion, plus or minus 3 percent, above the roughly $16.2 billion analysts expected. Chief executive Lisa Su also told analysts the company could grow revenue by more than 80 percent in 2027, well above its previous long-term ambition of 35 percent or more — a forecast, not a result, but one analysts said could imply more than $94 billion in 2027 revenue. The next test for the AI trade comes with Nvidia's earnings on November 17, reports noted.

articles.title: Arista Revenue Jumps 58.5% to $3.66 Billion, Its Fastest Growth Since the IPO
articles.description: Arista Networks reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58.5% — its fastest growth since going public — and gave a first 2027 forecast of about $18.5 billion, sending shares up about 9% after hours.
articles.sources: Arista earnings release via TickerRoast, MarketBeat, Dow Jones via Morningstar, November 3-4, 2026
articles.body:
Arista Networks reported its fastest revenue growth since its 2014 initial public offering on Tuesday, November 3, as spending on the networks connecting AI accelerators kept accelerating, with shares rising about 9 percent in after-hours trading, reports said.

The quarter

Revenue for the quarter ended September 30 reached $3.6576 billion, up 58.5 percent from $2.3083 billion a year earlier and up 20.5 percent from the second quarter, beating Arista's own guidance of about $3.3 billion and the roughly $3.33 billion analysts expected. GAAP net income rose to $1.56 billion from $853 million, and adjusted earnings were $1.20 per share against a $1.08 estimate. Chief executive Jayshree Ullal called it “another momentous quarter with the highest year-over-year revenue growth since our IPO and record profitability.”

The 2027 outlook

For the fourth quarter, Arista forecast revenue of $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion, above the roughly $3.6 billion analysts expected, and raised its 2026 revenue outlook for the fourth time to about $13.3 billion. On the earnings call, Ullal gave a first look at 2027: revenue growth of 38 to 40 percent, to about $18.5 billion, with AI networking expected to roughly double to about $7 billion. Those are forecasts, and the stock had already fallen more than 20 percent from its October high before the report.

articles.title: Apple Posts Record $114.5 Billion Quarter — Then Shares Fall on Margin Warning
articles.description: Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12%, beating Wall Street estimates — but shares fell about 3% after hours as it guided holiday-quarter margins down to 45-46% on rising memory costs.
articles.sources: Apple press release, Reuters, 9to5Mac, Invezz, November 2-3, 2026
articles.body:
Apple reported its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results on Monday, November 2, after the market closed, posting quarterly revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year over year, and diluted earnings per share of $2.10, up 14 percent — both ahead of Wall Street expectations of about $113.4 billion and $1.99, Apple and Reuters reported.

A record quarter, led by iPhone and Services

iPhone revenue rose about 17 percent to a September-quarter record of $57.58 billion, Mac revenue rose 24 percent to $10.8 billion, and Services revenue reached a new all-time high of $31.57 billion. Gross margin was 47.9 percent, including a favourable impact of about one percentage point from tariff refunds. Full-year revenue reached a record $479 billion, and the board declared a dividend of $0.27 per share, payable November 16 to shareholders of record on November 12.

Why the stock fell anyway

On the earnings call, chief executive John Ternus — in his first call since succeeding Tim Cook on September 1 — called current memory-price increases unprecedented and expected them to worsen. Apple guided December-quarter gross margin to 45 to 46 percent, down from 47.9 percent, and Services growth of 8 to 9 percent, below the 10.7 percent analysts expected, while still forecasting 7 to 10 percent total revenue growth, which would be a record holiday quarter. Shares fell as much as 4.43 percent during the call before recovering to close after hours down about 2.8 percent at $328.81.

articles.title: Palantir Revenue Jumps 96% to $2.31 Billion as US Commercial Sales Pass Government
articles.description: Palantir reported third-quarter revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% year over year, beating estimates — with US commercial revenue of $984 million passing US government revenue of $953 million for the first time.
articles.sources: Motley Fool, CNBC via Seoul Economic Daily, Ad-hoc News, November 2-3, 2026
articles.body:
Palantir Technologies reported third-quarter 2026 results on Monday, November 2, with revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96 percent year over year and above the roughly $2.18 billion consensus estimate, as its artificial intelligence software demand accelerated, reports said.

A milestone in the business mix

US commercial revenue surged 148 percent year over year to $984 million, passing US government revenue of $953 million, up 96 percent, for the first time in the company's history. Total US revenue reached $1.937 billion, up 119 percent, and GAAP net income more than doubled to $1.128 billion. Adjusted earnings per share were $0.44, ahead of the $0.41 consensus, and adjusted operating income was $1.427 billion, a 62 percent margin.

Guidance raised — but shares still fell

Palantir raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $8.530 to $8.534 billion, up from $8.150 to $8.158 billion, and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $2.649 to $2.653 billion. Despite the beat and the raise, shares fell in premarket trading on Tuesday, with analysts pointing to slowing total contract value growth — total contract value rose just 6 percent year over year to $2.918 billion — and to a broader repricing of high-valuation AI names.

articles.title: Apple's $113 Billion Earnings Test: What to Watch in Ternus's First Call
articles.description: Apple reports fiscal fourth-quarter results after Monday's close, with Wall Street expecting about $113.4 billion in revenue and $1.99 per share — the first earnings call for chief executive John Ternus.
articles.sources: Reuters, TipRanks, EBC, Coinpaper, November 2, 2026
articles.body:
Apple reports its fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 results on Monday, November 2, after the market closes, in what investors see as a crucial test for the AI-era market after October's selloff erased more than $2 trillion in Nasdaq-100 value, reports said.

What Wall Street expects

Analysts expect revenue of about $113.4 billion, up nearly 11 percent from $102.47 billion a year earlier, and earnings of about $1.99 per share, up from $1.85. IPhone revenue is projected at about $56.5 billion, up roughly 15 percent, though the quarter captures only nine days of iPhone 18 Pro sales; the foldable iPhone Duo, launched October 23, falls into the December quarter. Services revenue is expected at about $31.7 billion, and Apple guided gross margin of 47 to 48 percent, down from 50.1 percent in the prior quarter as memory costs rise.

Why this call matters

The report will be chief executive John Ternus's first earnings call since succeeding Tim Cook on September 1. Investors will focus on holiday-quarter guidance — analysts project about $153 billion in December-quarter revenue — and on whether Apple's lighter AI spending, which helped it pass Nvidia as the world's most valuable company at $5.03 trillion on Friday, can keep delivering growth while rivals face scrutiny over data-center costs.

articles.title: Palantir's $2.18 Billion Earnings Test After a 6% Pre-Report Slide
articles.description: Palantir reports third-quarter results after Monday's close, with Wall Street expecting about $2.18 billion in revenue — after shares fell 6.27% on Friday to $184.11 ahead of the print.
articles.sources: TradingKey, Stocktwits, Tickeron, Bitget, November 2, 2026
articles.body:
Palantir Technologies reports third-quarter 2026 results after the US market closes on Monday, November 2, in one of the week's most watched tests of whether AI software demand can justify premium valuations, reports said.

The high bar

Wall Street expects revenue of about $2.18 billion, up roughly 84 to 85 percent year over year, and adjusted earnings of about $0.41 per share, nearly double the $0.21 of a year earlier. That consensus sits slightly above the company's own guidance of $2.160 to $2.164 billion. The key watch items are US commercial revenue — which surged 149 percent to $764 million in the second quarter — government revenue, expected near $1.04 billion, and any change to full-year guidance, currently $8.150 to $8.158 billion.

A stock under pressure

Palantir shares fell 6.27 percent on Friday to close at $184.11, about 14 percent below a record high near $213, as investors cut risk in high-valuation AI names. The stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio near 90 to 97 times, far above most large software companies. Oppenheimer raised its price target to $235 from $200 last week, while JPMorgan initiated coverage with an Overweight rating and a $262 target — but analysts warn that even a beat may not be enough in a market repricing AI spending.

articles.title: Apple Passes Nvidia as World's Most Valuable Company at $5.03 Trillion
articles.description: Apple closed Friday worth $5.03 trillion, edging past Nvidia's $4.93 trillion, as investors rewarded companies spending less on AI data centers ahead of Apple's earnings report on Monday.
articles.sources: Bloomberg via The Seattle Times, US Brief, October 30-31, 2026
articles.body:
Apple ended Friday, October 30, as the world's most valuable public company, edging past Nvidia as investors moved away from companies spending heavily on artificial intelligence, Bloomberg reported.

The changing of the guard

Apple's shares fell 1.2% on Friday, leaving it worth $5.03 trillion, while Nvidia's shares fell 4.2%, cutting the chipmaker's value to $4.93 trillion. It is the first time Apple has held the top spot since a brief stint in late July, and it comes three days before Apple reports results. The swap is a sign that investors are now rewarding companies for spending less on AI rather than more — a reversal from much of the past two years of the AI boom. Apple shares are up 27% this year, more than twice Nvidia's gain, and Apple has kept its capital spending down while its free cash flow is projected to rise 38% to $142 billion for its fiscal year that ended September 30.

Why the AI trade is wobbling

The rotation follows weak results from the biggest AI spenders: Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion for the third quarter, and Amazon reported a $42.4 billion shortfall over the past 12 months, while Intel plunged 29% on Friday after weak guidance. Nvidia sells the chips that power AI data centers, so doubts about whether that spending will pay off hit it directly. Whether Apple keeps the crown likely depends on its earnings report on Monday, November 2 — its first under chief executive John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook on September 1.

articles.title: Apple and Alibaba Bring Qwen AI to Apple Intelligence in China
articles.description: Apple and Alibaba announced on October 31 a partnership to integrate Alibaba's Qwen model into Apple Intelligence, with testing opening for Chinese users with the iOS developer beta on November 4.
articles.sources: Longbridge, October 31, 2026
articles.body:
Apple and Alibaba announced on October 31 a partnership to integrate Qwen, Alibaba's artificial intelligence model, into Apple Intelligence for users in China, according to reports on the announcement.

What Chinese users will get

Chinese users will be able to use Qwen's text and image understanding, content generation and other capabilities within Siri, writing tools and visual intelligence. The features will open for testing with the latest iOS developer beta starting November 4 and are set to launch officially for Chinese users with the release of iOS 27.3 in December.

Why the partnership matters

Apple has previously relied on partnerships to bring AI features to markets where its own models face regulatory or competitive constraints, and China is one of its largest markets. The Qwen integration arrives days before Apple reports quarterly earnings on Monday, November 2, when investors will be watching for signs of demand for its devices and AI features. The announcement is a partnership disclosure, not a product launch: the features remain in testing until the December software release.

articles.title: Nasdaq Suffers Worst Day Since June as Intel Plunges 29% on AI Spending Fears
articles.description: The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% on Friday to close at 25,437, its biggest one-day drop since June, as Intel's weak outlook deepened investor doubts about the payoff from massive AI spending.
articles.sources: Reuters via Moneycontrol, Bilyonaryo, Indian Economic Observer, October 31, 2026
articles.body:
Wall Street ended October on a weak note on Friday, with the Nasdaq Composite recording its biggest daily percentage decline since June as investors reassessed the scale of artificial intelligence spending by major technology companies, Reuters reported on October 31.

Intel leads a broad chip selloff

Intel shares plunged 28.6% after its weak fourth-quarter guidance, while Reddit fell about 29% and memory-chip maker SanDisk dropped 13%. Nvidia fell 4.2% and AMD about 10.9%, and the broader semiconductor index declined 7.2%, taking its monthly losses to more than 15%. Server makers Dell and HP also came under pressure, falling 10.8% and 9.6% respectively.

The four so-called hyperscalers — Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Alphabet — fell 1% to 2% on Friday after significant declines earlier in the week. Capital Economics noted they have been responsible for more than a third of all capital spending by current S&P 500 constituents over the past 12 months, a share that looks likely to rise further, a prospect investors are struggling with.

A correction in the making

The Nasdaq Composite is now down 7.8% from its record closing high reached on October 6, and the Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5% on Friday, putting it on the brink of a 10% correction from its recent high. October was the technology sector's worst month since March 2025. As one strategist told Reuters, the week has been very much about the future of AI and whether there will be a positive return on investment — and if so, how quickly.

articles.title: AI Giants Pledge a Single 'No Scraping' Tool for Publishers After Years of Complaints
articles.description: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic pledged on Friday to give websites a single standardized way to block their content from being scraped to train AI models.
articles.sources: AFP via Malay Mail, October 31, 2026
articles.body:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic pledged on Friday to give media outlets and other websites a single way to prevent their content from being scraped to train artificial intelligence models, amid growing criticism and legal battles from news publishers, AFP reported on October 31.

One instruction instead of many

Publishers currently have to implement multiple blocking commands for every bot that crawls the web to collect data. The new proposed solution will let them enter a single, standardized instruction recognized and honored by any AI company that adopts the protocol. The announcement comes as publishers face a surge in bots scraping their articles to feed AI models, and as some, like the New York Times, have taken the matter to court — the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023, alleging millions of its articles were used without authorization or payment to train ChatGPT.

A slow rollout, with limits

The solution will not fully take effect for months. Microsoft will implement it beginning February 1, 2027, and Google sometime in 2027; OpenAI said it will roll it out in the coming months, while Anthropic said it has already started. The setting will apply only to future training of models, does not prevent bots from crawling otherwise, and content scraping will be allowed by default until a publisher changes the setting, Microsoft said in a blog post.

articles.title: Amazon's AWS Jumps 39% to $46 Billion, but a $42.4 Billion Cash Outflow Sinks the Stock
articles.description: Amazon missed profit and sales estimates in the third quarter despite AWS growing 39% to $46 billion, as AI spending pushed trailing free cash flow to a $42.4 billion outflow and shares fell sharply.
articles.sources: CNBC, Skimwire, Briefing.com, Economic Times, October 30, 2026
articles.body:
Amazon reported third-quarter results late on Thursday, October 29, and the market's verdict was swift: shares fell nearly 7% in after-hours trading and about 6% in Friday premarket trading, even as its cloud division posted its fastest growth in nearly five years.

AWS accelerates, the rest of the company lags

Amazon Web Services brought in $46 billion in the quarter ended September 30, up 39.3% from a year earlier and ahead of analyst expectations of about $45.3 billion, according to CNBC. AWS operating income rose 55% to $17.8 billion, putting the business at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate. Chief executive Andy Jassy said AWS could grow more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028.

The wider company was softer. Total sales rose 12% to $201.9 billion, missing expectations of about $202.3 billion, while earnings per share of $1.89 missed the $1.96 consensus. Net income slipped to $20.7 billion from $21.2 billion, mostly because last year's quarter included a $9.5 billion gain on Amazon's Anthropic stake. Amazon said growth would have been about four points higher if Prime Day had not moved into the second quarter.

The cash-flow problem

The deeper worry is spending. Trailing free cash flow swung from a $14.8 billion inflow a year ago to a $42.4 billion outflow, as capital spending reached $75.9 billion in the quarter alone and about $220 billion is expected for the full year. Long-term debt rose to $173.1 billion from $65.6 billion at year-end, while quarterly interest expense more than tripled to $1.69 billion, according to Briefing.com.

For the holiday quarter, Amazon guided to sales of $240 billion to $247 billion, with the midpoint below the $244.5 billion analysts expected, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion. Jassy also said Amazon will sell its Trainium AI chips outside AWS. The pattern now matches the week's other big tech reports: cloud growth is strong, but investors are asking harder questions about who pays for the AI buildout — and when it pays back.

articles.title: Intel Plunges About 25% as Weak Fourth-Quarter Guidance Overshadows a Third-Quarter Beat
articles.description: Intel beat third-quarter expectations but guided to fourth-quarter revenue of about $15.5 billion and adjusted earnings of 25 cents, far below Wall Street forecasts, sending shares down roughly 25% in premarket trading.
articles.sources: FXStreet, Invezz, Economic Times, October 30, 2026
articles.body:
Intel delivered the week's second big earnings shock on Friday, October 30, plunging about 25% in premarket trading after a fourth-quarter outlook that fell far short of expectations, even though its third-quarter results beat forecasts.

Guidance, not the quarter, did the damage

Intel guided to fourth-quarter revenue of about $15.5 billion at the midpoint, well below the roughly $17 billion analysts expected, and adjusted earnings per share of $0.25 against a $0.44 consensus, according to FXStreet and Invezz. The miss follows Alphabet's post-earnings plunge on Thursday and Amazon's selloff, sealing a brutal week for AI-linked stocks.

Analysts pointed to three pressures behind the warning: weak PC demand, manufacturing constraints, and heavy investment in expanding production that is expected to burn cash this year. The combination, they said, is exactly the setup where investors keep de-risking until guidance stabilizes.

Part of a wider AI selloff

The Intel warning deepened Friday's broader rout: Nasdaq futures fell more than 2%, Nvidia dropped about 3% and AMD about 8.7% in early trading, while Alphabet extended its losses after its record selloff. The selloff has reframed the AI trade for now: investors are no longer rewarding growth alone, but demanding proof that massive infrastructure spending turns into cash — and punishing any company whose outlook suggests it will not, at least not soon.

articles.title: Microsoft Rises, Alphabet Falls: Free Cash Flow Becomes the AI Earnings Scorecard
articles.description: Microsoft shares rose and Alphabet's fell after both reported on October 28, as investors rewarded Microsoft's $18.6 billion free cash flow and punished Alphabet's $9.1 billion shortfall.
articles.sources: CNBC, Aju Press, Yahoo Finance reports, October 28-29, 2026
articles.body:
Two of the world's biggest technology companies reported earnings on the same night, and the market delivered a split verdict. Microsoft shares rose about 4% in after-hours trading on October 28, while Alphabet shares fell about 10%, after results that showed how differently the two giants are funding the artificial intelligence buildout.

Microsoft beats on revenue, profit and cash

Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% from a year earlier, beating analyst expectations, with adjusted earnings per share of $4.89 against a $4.73 consensus. Azure revenue grew 48% to $33.2 billion, and the company generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow despite spending $45.2 billion on AI capital expenditures. Chief executive Satya Nadella said the company is driving innovation in the cost-performance curve so customers can turn tokens into business outcomes.

Alphabet's cloud doubles, but cash flow turns negative

Alphabet's Google Cloud revenue jumped 103% to $30.7 billion, more than twice Azure's growth rate, yet the company missed expectations for revenue, earnings per share and search advertising. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures, more than its operating cash flow, producing a free cash flow deficit of about $9.1 billion — its second consecutive negative quarter and its first such deficits since going public in 2004, according to reports on the results.

What comes next

The contrast has reframed how investors judge AI spending: not by how fast cloud revenue grows, but by whether the spending generates cash. Alphabet's shortfall, covered in part by bond sales and stock issuance, reignited the debate over AI returns. The test continues Thursday, when Amazon reports after the market close, with AWS growth and capital spending in focus.

articles.title: Nvidia Puts $3 Billion Into Meta as AI Partnership Deepens — and 'Circular' Worries Grow
articles.description: Nvidia will invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering as the two companies expand their Muse AI partnership, a deal critics say blurs the line between supplier and customer.
articles.sources: Reuters, GlobeNewswire, NewsGhana, October 27-29, 2026
articles.body:
Nvidia will invest $3 billion in Meta Platforms' equity offering, the companies announced on October 27, deepening a partnership that ties the world's leading AI chipmaker ever closer to one of its largest customers.

What the expanded deal covers

Under the expanded collaboration, Meta will deploy more Nvidia infrastructure, including next-generation Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs, alongside Spectrum-X networking and BlueField-4 technology, to train and run its Muse family of AI models. The companies said they will work together on improving training and inference performance, and are exploring Nvidia's OpenShell architecture and Sentry tools for safer deployment of AI agents. Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said the goal is delivering personal AI assistance to billions of people.

A record fundraising, with suppliers among the buyers

The investment forms part of Meta's expanded fundraising to pay for AI infrastructure, with reports putting the total offering at about $97.5 billion after an upsizing. Nvidia is not the only supplier buying in: AMD said it would invest $1 billion, and its Helios rack-scale systems are now running at Meta. Meta has projected capital spending of up to $145 billion this year and has warned it will need to raise hundreds of billions more over several years.

The circular-financing debate

Critics argue the arrangement is circular: a supplier invests in a customer, which then spends the money on the supplier's products, making it harder to tell how much AI demand comes from customers spending their own money. Supporters counter that Nvidia's processors remain the dominant hardware in AI data centers, supply remains tight relative to demand, and the investment is small next to the company's scale. Chip stocks rose on the news on October 28, but the debate over who ultimately pays for the AI buildout is only getting louder.

articles.title: SK Hynix Profit Jumps More Than Sevenfold as AI Rally Faces Earnings Test
articles.description: South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix reported a more than sevenfold rise in quarterly operating profit, adding fuel to the AI rally hours before Alphabet and Microsoft report earnings.
articles.sources: Free Malaysia Today, Malay Mail/AFP, October 28, 2026
articles.body:
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix reported a more than sevenfold rise in quarterly operating profit, giving the artificial intelligence trade a fresh jolt ahead of a decisive round of big-tech earnings. Shares in the company rose about 3% shortly after the open before paring gains to around 1.75% higher.

A rally waiting for proof

Asian markets rallied on the news, with South Korea's KOSPI jumping more than 3% and the MSCI Asia-Pacific index outside Japan up 0.85% in early trade. In the United States, the AI rally faces its next test after the market close on Wednesday, when Alphabet and Microsoft report earnings, with investors looking for evidence that heavy AI infrastructure spending is turning into sustainable revenue.

"While we're expecting strong results across the board, the focus is less about the actual earnings results than about whether the capex spending for AI growth will translate into sustainable revenue growth," said SWBC chief investment officer Chris Brigati. A series of AI funding announcements from Meta, SpaceX and Broadcom this week, plus Anthropic's IPO filing, has already breathed new life into the trade after a rocky stretch in which investors worried that AI investments might not pay off.

The earnings season is therefore doing double duty: it must justify both the chipmakers' valuations and the trillions being poured into data centres. SK Hynix cleared its bar. Whether the American giants do the same will set the tone for the rest of the week.

articles.title: Judge Orders OpenAI to Disclose Apple Hiring Records in Talent Dispute
articles.description: A federal judge ordered OpenAI to produce Apple hiring records by November 11, narrowing Apple's discovery demands in the bitter AI talent war.
articles.sources: Wisevoter court report, October 28, 2026
articles.body:
A federal judge has ordered OpenAI to disclose records related to its hiring of Apple employees, in a ruling that sharpens the legal scrutiny around the artificial intelligence industry's aggressive war for talent. Judge Edward Davila issued the discovery order on October 28, 2026, and OpenAI must comply by November 11, 2026.

Narrowed, not denied

The order follows Apple's narrowed requests for records. While the company must document its efforts to prevent the misuse of confidential information, the court denied Apple's broader request for access to internal investigations, marking a departure from the wider discovery Apple had originally sought. Former Apple employee Tang Tan is central to the dispute over talent acquisition and confidential information handling.

The ruling follows standard federal discovery rules but signals that companies can expect stricter judicial requirements to document internal data safeguards during periods of rapid staff turnover. For an industry built on poaching specialised researchers, that paperwork may soon matter as much as the paychecks.

articles.title: Apple Unveils M6 MacBook Pro and iMac With Faster On-Device AI
articles.description: Apple launched a new 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac powered by its M6 chip, touting faster graphics and on-device AI performance ahead of an October 28 event in Los Angeles.
articles.sources: Reuters
articles.body:
Apple on Tuesday unveiled a new 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac powered by its latest M6 chip, pitching faster performance for running artificial intelligence tasks directly on the devices rather than in the cloud. The launches arrive a day before Apple hosts an event in Los Angeles on October 28, which Bloomberg News has reported is expected to feature the company's first touch-screen MacBook Pro.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, while the new iMac starts at $1,499, according to Reuters. Customers can pre-order both products from Wednesday in 35 countries and regions, including the United States, with availability starting November 6.

What the M6 promises

Apple said the M6 MacBook Pro delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to 25 percent faster AI performance than its M5 predecessor, along with up to 24 hours of battery life, which the company described as the longest ever in a Mac. The new iMac delivers up to five times faster on-device AI performance than the previous M4 model, Apple said.

The emphasis on on-device AI reflects a broader industry shift toward running AI features locally, where tasks such as image processing, transcription, and writing assistance can run without sending data to remote servers. Apple has positioned its chips as central to that strategy, pairing faster neural processing with the power efficiency that has become a hallmark of its in-house silicon.

Ahead of the Los Angeles event

The M6 launches set the stage for Apple's October 28 event in Los Angeles, which the company has billed as a showcase event. Bloomberg News has reported that the event is expected to feature Apple's first touch-screen MacBook Pro, a product long requested by some Mac users but previously resisted by the company. Apple has not confirmed the details of what will be shown at the event.

The timing also places Apple's hardware announcements in the middle of a busy week for big technology companies, with several major firms due to report quarterly earnings in the coming days. Investors will be watching for signs of whether heavy AI spending is translating into growth, and hardware launches that showcase AI capabilities are part of how Apple makes its case to consumers and developers alike.

articles.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-6.1 Terra With Lower API Prices
articles.description: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra for ChatGPT Work, Codex and its API on October 26, offering a lower-priced model for work involving images and computer applications.
articles.sources: OpenAI model documentation via Okay News
articles.body:
OpenAI has released GPT-6.1 Terra, a new model for ChatGPT Work, Codex and its API, offering lower standard pricing than its GPT-6.1 Sol sibling for work involving images and computer applications. The model launched on October 26, 2026, and is available to Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, with developer access through the API under the identifier gpt-6.1-terra.

According to OpenAI's model documentation, standard charges for GPT-6.1 Terra are $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens and $5 per million output tokens. Tokens are the units used to measure how much text and data a model processes. Those rates apply to prompts containing no more than 272,000 input tokens; longer prompts attract double input and cache rates and 1.5 times the output rate for the full request, with cache writes and some tools carrying separate charges.

Built for computer use and coding

OpenAI reported improvements in computer-use and coding benchmarks for the new model, though those results are the company's own evaluations rather than independent tests. The model is aimed at work that involves images and computer applications, a growing area as AI assistants take on more multi-step tasks inside software, browsers and development tools.

The launch continues a pattern in which AI providers offer a range of models at different price and capability levels, letting developers and businesses pick the tradeoff that fits a given task. Lower-priced models are typically used for high-volume work where cost matters most, while more capable models handle tasks that demand greater accuracy or reasoning.

Part of a fast-moving model race

The release comes during a period of rapid model iteration across the industry, with providers competing on price, speed and specialized capabilities. For developers, the practical question is often not which model is most powerful in absolute terms but which one delivers the right performance at a sustainable cost for production workloads.

GPT-6.1 Terra's positioning as a lower-priced option for image and computer-application work suggests OpenAI is targeting exactly that calculation. The model documentation lists no support for the free API tier, meaning access runs through paid plans and API accounts.

articles.title: Musk Says SpaceX Closed $40 Billion in GPU Debt and Warns of a Neocloud Shakeout
articles.description: Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed $40 billion of debt to buy GPUs, and warned that more than 200 neocloud companies face consolidation as lending tightens.
articles.sources: SiliconANGLE, Financial Times, AI News Online
articles.body:
Elon Musk said over the weekend that SpaceX has closed $40 billion of debt to buy graphics processing units, and warned that the crowded field of companies renting out GPU capacity faces a brutal shakeout as credit markets tighten.

In a post on X, Musk said the debt will fund chips due in the first and second quarters of 2027, and that he expects most of it to be repaid early. He credited SpaceX's investment-grade rating and its Starlink and launch revenue for getting the deal done. He did not name the lenders, though the Financial Times reported on October 7 that Apollo led the financing. Interest rates and other terms have not been disclosed.

Credit is drying up for AI data centers

Musk wrote that debt markets have almost entirely shut off money for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers. That warning lands at a moment when cheap credit has paid for much of the AI build-out, and tighter lending could slow construction of new capacity.

The companies most exposed are the so-called neoclouds, firms that rent out GPU capacity to AI developers. Musk said the more than 200 neoclouds in the market face what he called guppy-level death and consolidation, a phrase that quickly spread across tech and market coverage on Monday.

Neocloud stocks slide on Monday

The warning appeared to weigh on neocloud stocks in premarket trading on Monday. CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren were reported down 2.4 percent, 1.9 percent and 1.8 percent respectively in early trading, as investors reassessed which GPU-rental businesses can survive a funding squeeze.

At the same time, SpaceX shares were reported up modestly, a sign that markets are drawing a sharp line between companies with diversified revenue and those dependent entirely on AI infrastructure demand.

Why it matters this week

The financing debate arrives just as the biggest spenders in AI prepare to report earnings. Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon all report later this week, and investors will be listening closely for how much they plan to keep spending on chips and data centers, and how they plan to pay for it.

Data center tenants are also pushing more risk onto developers. Tenants now demand late-delivery penalties of $5 million or more a day, up from about $1 million this spring, according to a report from The Information, and insurance brokers have begun offering delay-in-delivery coverage for developers facing those penalties.

Together, the credit squeeze and the rising penalties paint a tougher picture for the AI infrastructure boom: the money is getting more expensive, the deadlines are getting more punishing, and only the best-capitalized players may be able to keep building at full speed.

articles.title: AI Inference Prices Have Fallen as Much as 80 Percent Since June, Analysis Finds
articles.description: OpenAI and Anthropic have quietly cut inference prices by up to 80 percent since June, driven by Chinese competition, better efficiency and perishable GPU capacity, according to a new analysis.
articles.sources: AI0 News, minimaxir analysis, The Register
articles.body:
The price of running artificial intelligence models has collapsed in recent months. OpenAI and Anthropic have quietly cut inference prices by up to 80 percent since June, according to an analysis of the June to September price slide, turning one of the industry's biggest cost centers into a fast-moving bargain for developers.

Inference, the cost of actually running a trained model to answer questions or write code, is where most AI spending now lands. When those prices fall this sharply, the economics of building AI products change for startups, enterprises and hobbyists alike.

What drove the price collapse

The analysis points to three forces. The first is Chinese competition: DeepSeek's Flash V4 model is reported to earn about $38 per GPU per hour while charging $0.60 per million output tokens, a price point that puts pressure on every Western lab. The second is better inference efficiency, as labs squeeze more work out of the same hardware. The third is the simple fact that GPU capacity is perishable, like airline seats: an idle chip earns nothing, so providers would rather cut prices than leave capacity unused.

Cache-read reductions matter disproportionately for agentic coding, where cached context can account for 70 to 75 percent of total cost, the analysis notes, which helps explain why coding-focused workloads have seen some of the steepest savings.

IBM says open models now cost a tenth as much on-premises

IBM chief executive Arvind Krishna told investors that open-weight models have closed the gap enough to make small on-premises deployments compelling for routine work such as email summarization and contract review, at about 10 percent of the cost of frontier models, according to The Register.

Independent developers appear to agree. Commenters discussing the price analysis said some have not paid for a frontier model in months, with open models paired with strong advisors now feeling close to top-tier performance for everyday tasks. Others cautioned that Krishna is, in part, talking his own book, since IBM would like to sell the accelerator hardware that runs those on-premises deployments.

A race to the bottom, or a gift to builders?

Observers are split on what the price war means. Some see a race to the bottom in which somebody eventually goes bankrupt. Others see exactly the outcome competition is supposed to produce: cheaper intelligence for everyone, with labs turning to regulation and differentiated features to defend their margins.

One notable side effect is that both OpenAI and Anthropic have grown more interested in regulation as prices fall, a shift that some analysts read as an effort to slow a commoditization trend they can no longer control with pricing alone.

For now, the practical takeaway for businesses is clear: the cost of running AI has rarely been lower, and contracts signed even a few months ago may already be out of date. Companies renegotiating AI deals this quarter have a strong case for demanding the new, lower rates.

articles.title: White House Names Jay Clayton as AI Czar to Lead 'Super Intelligence Force'
articles.description: President Trump tapped Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force with 120 days to report on risks, opportunities and the government's role.
articles.sources: Associated Press via Broadband Breakfast, Nextgov, GovCIO Media
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has tapped Jay Clayton, his director of national intelligence, to lead a new government task force on artificial intelligence. Trump is calling it the “Super Intelligence Force,” part of his effort to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” and the announcement on Sunday, October 4, 2026, came after Trump hosted top executives of AI companies at the White House the previous week.

The task force will coordinate the federal effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a social media post announcing the move. It will reach out to consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies.

Who is on the task force

Clayton, who was confirmed as intelligence chief in August after previously serving as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and as chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission, replaces former AI and crypto czar David Sacks, who served part time and stepped down in March after reaching his allotted 130 days. Sacks now joins as an external adviser, alongside former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, according to Nextgov.

The task force's three vice chairs are Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. Its members include Vice President JD Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and the group reports directly to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

A 120-day clock — and a security-first signal

Under its charter, the task force has 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities of advanced AI and to set out a federal plan, including plans to handle AI-enabled threats, streamline breach notifications and improve government response capacity while aiming to avoid overregulation. Putting the sitting intelligence chief at the helm signals that the administration treats AI leadership as a national security question as much as an economic one. Clayton framed the stakes bluntly to the Wall Street Journal: “The risk of not being first is high.”

The task force follows an earlier White House step: Trump hosted AI company executives last week and said they had signed a voluntary accord that would effectively self-police the development of the technology, according to the Associated Press. The administration has also begun referring to AI as “super intelligence” after the president signed an executive order late last month calling for federal agencies to use the new phrasing, Nextgov reported. Critics, including Senator Mark Warner, have questioned how much authority the new body actually has — a question the task force's 120-day report will have to answer in practice, not just on paper.

articles.title: SpaceX Q3 2026: $14.6 Billion Revenue as Starship Flight 15 Targets a Dual-Stage Catch
articles.description: SpaceX revenue jumped 161% year over year to $14.6 billion, Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers, and Flight 15 will attempt to catch both the booster and the ship.
articles.sources: SpaceX Q3 2026 results, Tesla Oracle, TradingKey, KuCoin
articles.body:
SpaceX delivered revenue of $14.6 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 161% year over year, the company reported on October 20, 2026, with income from operations of $2.8 billion, net income of $4.4 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $8.8 billion. The quarter marked what the company described as an inflection moment across launch, connectivity and its Super Intelligence business.

Super Intelligence is now SpaceX's largest segment. Revenue reached $7.56 billion, up 830% year over year, driven by the activation of new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor — which contributed $608 million after its August 14 close — and growing adoption of Grok. Connectivity revenue rose 69% year over year to $5.25 billion, and Starlink ended the quarter with 13.6 million consumer subscribers, up 1.6 million, at $69 a month average revenue per user.

Starship goes commercial

Starship Flight 14 was the company's first revenue-generating Starship mission, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites and adding roughly ten times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch. SpaceX completed 35 launches in the quarter, including 21 Starlink Falcon 9 flights, two Starship flights, one Falcon Heavy mission and 12 customer missions. Nameplate compute reached 1.7 gigawatts as of September 30, as the company builds out Colossus II in Memphis.

The next milestone is the most ambitious yet. Musk said Starship Flight 15, expected in November, will try to catch both the booster and the ship at the tower — which would be the first time an orbital rocket has been fully recovered. Management said it plans to pursue weekly Starship flights during the first half of 2027 and potentially twice-weekly flights in the second half.

The spending behind the surge

The growth comes with extraordinary spending: capital expenditures totaled $19.6 billion in the quarter, with $16.4 billion allocated to the Super Intelligence segment. Starlink Mobile reached more than 22 million monthly users, and SpaceX received FCC approval to launch 15,000 Mobile V2 satellites. Whether the AI bet pays for itself is now the central question for the world's most valuable private space company — but on revenue alone, the third quarter was its biggest yet.

Two other numbers from the quarter show how broad the company has become. Grok Bot, launched in August, had 800,000 paid weekly users earlier in October, more than doubling in a month, and enterprise deployment is underway. Starlink Mobile reached more than 22 million monthly users, up 37% sequentially, and Starlink was contracted for approximately 12,000 aircraft, nearly one-quarter of the available aircraft referenced by management. The company also quadrupled aviation production capacity from the beginning of 2026 and expected to double it again before year-end — growth that helps explain why connectivity, once the whole story, is now only one of three engines.

articles.title: US Orders DeepSeek Stripped From Federal Civilian Systems
articles.description: A Department of Homeland Security order bars civilian agencies from buying DeepSeek products and requires removal of DeepSeek tools — including third-party services built on its models.
articles.sources: The Hacker News, Reuters via The Hindu BusinessLine, Federal Register (Docket DHS-2026-0628)
articles.body:
U.S. federal civilian agencies must remove DeepSeek products from their information technology systems, along with any third-party products or services “developed using DeepSeek implementations,” under a Department of Homeland Security order. They may also no longer buy IT products or services from the Chinese AI developer or its affiliates.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued the order, dated July 24, 2026, under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, and the department published it in the Federal Register on October 20, 2026, as Exclusion and Removal Order #2026-01 (Docket DHS-2026-0628). The order names Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., the developer of the R1 and V3 models, and covers its affiliates as defined in federal acquisition rules.

Why DHS acted

DHS said DeepSeek models pose “multiple threat vectors” and warned that use “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by U.S. government employees or vendors.” The department also said use of DeepSeek by government agencies “could produce actionable intelligence on US persons and/or government agencies” and that the models themselves “may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities.” DeepSeek's privacy policy says it collects, processes and stores users' personal data in the People's Republic of China.

The scope is what makes this order different from an ordinary procurement ban. Because it follows the model into third-party tools, agencies must audit not only DeepSeek's own products but anything built on its models — including low-cost tools employees or vendors may have adopted without treating them as Chinese AI at all. Agencies that need more time or a narrower scope must request an exception in writing.

What the order does not do

The order covers only what civilian agencies buy and run. It does not restrict companies or the public, and it does not by itself bind the Department of Defense or the intelligence community, which have their own issuing authorities under the 2018 law. The law was first used in 2025, when the Director of National Intelligence excluded Acronis from intelligence community procurement. For federal IT managers, though, the message is clear: provenance of AI models is now a supply-chain security question.

One practical problem remains unresolved: the notice does not define “DeepSeek implementations,” The Hacker News noted, which means agencies will need to ask suppliers whether their products fall under the ban. In a July memo made public alongside the order, DHS told federal agencies to monitor flows of traffic in and out of government websites to address potential risks from DeepSeek, Reuters reported. The order also carries an exception process requiring written requests with compelling justification — though some coverage noted the 60-day window for such requests had effectively elapsed before the public filing appeared, leaving agencies to seek clarity from DHS directly.
